item.title: Conveyancing blamed for property sales delays as buyers lose patience
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Delays in property transactions are increasingly being attributed to conveyancing, with many homebuyers expressing frustration over the process. According to recent research commissioned by Lyons Bowe, conveyancing is seen as a more significant hurdle than property chains, with 42% of respondents identifying it as the main barrier to a smooth sale. In comparison, just 19% cited chains as the primary issue.

The findings shine a light on communication between conveyancers, with 23% of respondents blaming slow exchanges between buyers’ and sellers’ legal representatives for delays. For estate agents navigating lengthy sales processes, the research also highlights differing expectations around who should drive transactions forward. While 49% believe conveyancers hold the greatest influence over a smooth progression, a third (33%) argue that responsibility should be shared equally among all parties involved.

Communication Challenges in Conveyancing

When asked what could have improved their most recent property transaction, 24% of buyers pointed to faster responses from conveyancers, while 20% called for better communication between all parties. Additionally, 17% said earlier access to legal and property information would have been beneficial. These responses suggest that many homebuyers feel left in the dark during the conveyancing stage, with 42% stating they had the least visibility at this point in the process.

This lack of clarity has led some buyers to advocate for changes to the conveyancing process itself. Almost a quarter (23%) of respondents said they would like to see the process shortened and simplified to improve the overall homebuying experience.

The Need for Transparency and Collaboration

Paul Lyons, managing director at Lyons Bowe Solicitors, commented on the findings, acknowledging the complexity of conveyancing while emphasising the importance of transparency. “Buying a home is a significant financial and emotional commitment,” he said. “It’s understandable that people want greater certainty about what is happening with their transaction and when they can expect it to progress.”

Lyons added that whilst conveyancing inherently involves legal complexities and relies on information from various parties, this doesn’t mean the process should feel opaque or unnecessarily challenging for clients. “An easy, smooth transaction is not simply about completing the legal work quickly,” he explained. “It’s about ensuring everyone involved has the information they need and that the client is kept informed throughout.”

Moving Forward

The research highlights the need for improved communication and collaboration across the property transaction process. For buyers, this means staying informed and proactive, whilst conveyancers and estate agents might consider adopting clearer communication strategies to keep clients updated. Simplifying certain aspects of conveyancing could also help reduce delays and improve the overall experience for homebuyers.

Ultimately, while conveyancing will always involve a degree of complexity, addressing communication gaps and enhancing transparency could go a long way in alleviating frustrations and ensuring smoother transactions for all parties involved.

item.title: Ex-estate agent launches UK’s first sales progression franchise
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A new franchise model aims to tackle the persistent delays in UK property transactions by offering specialist sales progression services to estate agents across England and Wales. Property Progressors, founded by former estate agent Natasha Candeias, has launched what it claims is Britain's first franchised sales progression business, creating opportunities for both agents and experienced property professionals.

Local expertise to speed up property sales

The company plans to establish a network of locally based sales progressors who will handle transactions from offer acceptance through to completion. Unlike traditional models where agents manage sales in-house, this approach provides dedicated specialists with capped caseloads of just 60 transactions at a time. Property Progressors reports this focused approach helps complete sales in an average of 78 days - notably faster than the typical 100-plus days seen across the wider market.

Candeias, drawing on 14 years of estate agency experience, highlights how local knowledge can prevent delays before they arise. A progressor familiar with their area will understand local search times, know which properties require additional documentation, and maintain relationships with solicitors who can help keep transactions on track when issues emerge.

Franchise opportunities for property professionals

The model offers two key benefits to the property sector. For estate agents, it provides an outsourced alternative to employing in-house progressors, with locally based specialists handling transactions in their area. For experienced sales progressors, the franchise presents an opportunity to run their own business while benefiting from the company's systems, customer relationship management tools and training.

Candeias notes that sales progression careers often face limitations within traditional agency structures: "This gives talented professionals somewhere to grow while keeping their valuable experience in the industry." The company aims to reduce the sector's high staff turnover among skilled progressors while simultaneously addressing the 30-36% fall-through rates currently affecting the market.

As Property Progressors expands its franchise network, both estate agents and home movers may benefit from more streamlined transactions with fewer delays. With completion times significantly below market averages, this specialist approach could help reduce stress for all parties involved in the often complex process of buying and selling property.

item.title: Rental hotspots revealed as homes attract up to 30 enquiries each
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The rental market in Britain continues to show signs of intense competition in certain areas, with some properties attracting as many as 30 enquiries during the summer months. According to recent analysis by Rightmove, the North West emerged as a dominant region for rental hotspots, with six of the top 10 most competitive locations situated in this area. Scotland also stood out, recording the highest regional level of competition.

Regional Rental Hotspots

Birkenhead and Wallasey, both located in the North West, topped the list of rental hotspots, with each available property receiving an average of 30 enquiries during July and August. Carlisle followed closely behind, with 29 enquiries per property, while Glasgow and East Kilbride in Scotland recorded 28 and 27 enquiries respectively. Notably, three of the six most competitive areas were found on the Wirral Peninsula, highlighting the region’s appeal to renters.

Across Great Britain, the average number of enquiries per rental property stood at 11 during the summer months. While this represents a slight decline from 12 enquiries during the same period in 2022, it remains higher than the pre-pandemic average of eight enquiries per property. Scotland led the way regionally, with an average of 19 enquiries per property, followed closely by the North West at 16.

Rental Market Trends

Despite the easing of competition in some areas, demand remains robust in certain hotspots. Rightmove’s analysis, which covered 1,000 locations across Great Britain, defines an enquiry as a prospective tenant contacting a letting agent to arrange a viewing. The findings suggest that whilst the rental market has rebalanced compared to previous years, certain locations continue to experience high levels of demand.

Average advertised rents across Britain currently stand at £1,580 per month. However, rental growth has slowed as increased supply provides tenants with more options. For example, properties in Birkenhead and Wallasey, despite their high levels of competition, have average rents of £874 and £975 per month respectively—significantly lower than the national average.

Colleen Babcock, Rightmove’s property expert, commented: “July and August are typically the busiest months for the rental market, and our analysis shows that competition remains particularly strong in some parts of Great Britain. While rental supply has improved compared to previous years, there are still locations where each available home attracts high numbers of enquiries.”

For those considering renting in a competitive area, it could be worth exploring properties early and being prepared to act quickly. Additionally, renters might wish to broaden their search to neighbouring areas, where demand may be slightly lower.

item.title: Estate agents urged to ‘act now’ on home moving reforms
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The property industry is being encouraged to proactively embrace upcoming changes to the home-moving process rather than waiting for mandatory requirements to take effect. Key figures from conveyancing and property data organisations recently highlighted the benefits of early adoption during a webinar hosted by LMS’s National Property Transaction Network (NPTN).

Why early engagement matters

Industry leaders emphasised that estate agents and conveyancers have a unique opportunity to shape forthcoming reforms by participating in current consultations and pilot schemes. The government’s home buying and selling reform roadmap outlines significant changes including digital property logbooks, standardised upfront information packs, and improved data sharing across transactions.

Maria Harris, Chair of the Open Property Data Association, stressed the importance of operational staff contributing to the development process: "Having frontline professionals involved ensures proposals reflect genuine transaction challenges rather than theoretical obstacles." This approach could help create more practical solutions that streamline the home-moving process for all parties.

Potential benefits for early adopters

Property professionals who begin implementing digital processes now may gain several advantages:

  • Reduced duplication of work through standardised information sharing
  • Less time spent chasing missing documentation from sellers
  • The opportunity to influence final regulations through practical feedback
  • Potential competitive edge in marketing properties with complete digital packs

Beth Rudolf from the Conveyancing Association urged industry participants to engage with ongoing initiatives: "This represents a significant opportunity to improve the transaction process – we need input from practitioners to ensure the solutions work in real-world scenarios."

The government’s phased approach will initially encourage voluntary adoption of digital sales packs before potentially making them mandatory. Leon Ifayemi of CFIT warned against last-minute implementation: "Proactive engagement now could prevent costly, rushed compliance later when regulations take full effect."

As the property sector moves towards digitised transactions, early adopters may find themselves better positioned to navigate the changing landscape. Industry professionals wishing to contribute to shaping these reforms can participate through various trade associations and government consultation channels.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property and mortgage sectors have seen notable developments recently, with industry veterans taking on key roles in prominent organisations. These appointments come at a time when the property market continues to evolve, with brokers and conveyancers adapting to changing demands and challenges.

Experienced Broker Joins Moveli

Rollo Miles, a seasoned property professional with over 25 years of experience in the London market, has joined Moveli as a West London broker. Miles, who previously founded and managed Agent & Homes, brings a wealth of expertise to the brokerage. His career includes roles at well-known firms such as John D Wood & Co., Marsh & Parsons, and Bective, giving him a deep understanding of the high-value residential property sector.

At Moveli, Miles will oversee the full spectrum of property transactions, from valuation and marketing to negotiation and completion. His appointment aligns with Moveli’s strategy to expand its network of self-employed agents, which now exceeds 100 brokers across London and regional markets. Ben Littlewood, Moveli’s co-founder and co-CEO, praised Miles’s unique blend of experience, noting his ability to excel as both an agent and a broker.

New Leadership for the Conveyancing Association

Nick Chadbourne, former CEO of LMS, has been appointed as the non-executive chair of the Conveyancing Association (CA). Chadbourne, who stepped down from LMS after a decade in leadership, brings extensive industry knowledge to the role. His background includes collaborations with lenders, conveyancers, mortgage advisers, and panel managers, positioning him well to address the challenges facing the conveyancing sector.

Chadbourne’s appointment comes amid potential reforms to the home buying and selling process. He has emphasised the importance of ensuring conveyancers have a voice in these changes. Additionally, he aims to tackle pressing issues such as fee levels, caseloads, and the loss of technical expertise as experienced professionals leave the industry. His immediate focus will be engaging with CA members and affiliates to establish long-term priorities.

These appointments highlight the ongoing evolution of the UK property and mortgage sectors. With experienced professionals like Miles and Chadbourne stepping into influential roles, the industry appears well-equipped to navigate the challenges and opportunities ahead.

item.title: Repossessed homes sell for 30% below average
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent research has revealed that repossessed homes in England are being listed for sale at prices approximately 30% lower than the average market value. With nearly 1,500 properties currently available, these homes could present potential opportunities for buyers seeking more affordable options in the property market.

Understanding Repossessed Properties

Repossessed homes are properties taken back by lenders when homeowners are unable to meet their mortgage repayments. These properties are often sold at a discount to ensure a quick sale, which can make them an attractive proposition for buyers. However, it’s important to note that purchasing a repossessed home can come with its own set of challenges, including potential maintenance issues or the need for renovations.

Opportunities for Buyers and Investors

For those looking to enter the property market or expand their investment portfolio, repossessed homes could be worth considering. The significant discount on asking prices may allow buyers to secure a property at a lower cost compared to other listings. Additionally, investors might find these properties appealing as they could offer potential for capital growth once refurbished or resold.

However, buyers should carefully assess the condition of the property and factor in any additional costs that may arise. It could also be beneficial to seek professional advice from a mortgage broker or property expert to ensure the purchase aligns with their financial goals.

Navigating the Process

Purchasing a repossessed property often involves a different process compared to traditional homebuying. These properties are typically sold through auctions or directly by lenders, which means buyers may need to act quickly and be prepared for competitive bidding. It’s also worth noting that some lenders may require proof of funds or a mortgage agreement in principle before proceeding.

Prospective buyers may wish to thoroughly research the local market and compare prices to ensure they are making an informed decision. Engaging a conveyancer or solicitor early in the process can also help streamline the transaction and address any legal complexities.

Repossessed homes offer a unique opportunity for buyers to secure properties at discounted prices, but they require careful consideration and preparation. By understanding the process and seeking professional guidance, homeowners and investors could find these listings a viable option in today’s property market.

item.title: Summer rental hotspots revealed
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

As summer approaches, rental markets across the UK are heating up, with certain regions experiencing particularly high demand from tenants. According to recent data from Rightmove, areas such as Merseyside and parts of Scotland have emerged as some of the most competitive rental hotspots in the country. This surge in interest highlights shifting trends in the rental market, as tenants seek out locations that offer affordability, accessibility, and lifestyle appeal.

Merseyside: A Rising Star for Renters

Merseyside has become a focal point for renters, driven by its combination of vibrant city living and more affordable rental prices compared to other major UK cities. Liverpool, in particular, continues to attract tenants with its thriving cultural scene, excellent transport links, and relatively lower cost of living. For landlords and property investors, this heightened demand could present opportunities, though tenants may face increased competition for available properties. Prospective renters might consider acting quickly to secure their preferred homes in this sought-after region.

Scotland’s Rental Market Gains Momentum

Scotland is also witnessing a surge in rental demand, with cities like Glasgow and Edinburgh leading the charge. Edinburgh’s appeal lies in its historic charm, world-class universities, and strong job market, making it a magnet for professionals and students alike. Meanwhile, Glasgow offers a more affordable alternative, with a growing reputation for its arts and music scene. Both cities are experiencing a tightening rental market, with properties being snapped up quickly. Renters in Scotland might find it beneficial to prepare their applications thoroughly and act decisively when opportunities arise.

What This Means for Tenants and Landlords

For tenants, the competitive nature of these rental hotspots underscores the importance of being well-prepared. Having essential documents ready, such as proof of income and references, could help speed up the application process. Additionally, staying informed about local rental trends might enable tenants to identify emerging areas with less competition.

For landlords, these hotspots represent potential opportunities to maximise rental yields. However, it’s crucial to ensure properties meet tenant expectations in terms of quality and amenities. Staying attuned to market demands could help landlords attract reliable tenants and minimise void periods.

As the summer rental market continues to evolve, both tenants and landlords may wish to stay informed about regional trends and act strategically to navigate the competitive landscape.

item.title: New BTL range offers 2.85% rate for landlords
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords looking to expand their property portfolios may find fresh opportunities as specialist lender Rely introduces a new range of buy-to-let (BTL) mortgage deals. The lender has expanded its product line-up, offering competitive fixed rates starting from 2.85% alongside a variety of fee options across multiple loan-to-value (LTV) tiers. This move could provide greater flexibility for property investors navigating the current market.

Competitive Rates for Buy-to-Let Investors

The headline rate of 2.85% is available across several fixed-term products, catering to landlords seeking stability in their mortgage repayments. With interest rates remaining a key consideration for many investors, these new deals could prove attractive, particularly for those looking to secure financing for additional properties. The range also includes options for higher LTVs, offering solutions for borrowers with varying levels of equity in their portfolios.

Flexible Fee Options

In addition to competitive rates, Rely’s new BTL range includes a choice of fee structures, allowing landlords to tailor their mortgages to suit their financial circumstances. Borrowers might consider opting for a lower arrangement fee in exchange for a slightly higher interest rate, or vice versa, depending on their long-term investment strategy. This flexibility could help investors manage upfront costs whilst optimising their overall mortgage expenses.

As the buy-to-let market continues to evolve, lenders like Rely are adapting their offerings to meet the changing needs of landlords. With competitive rates and flexible fee options, these new deals could provide a valuable opportunity for property investors looking to expand or refinance their portfolios. As always, it’s advisable to compare the full range of available products and seek independent financial advice to ensure the best fit for individual circumstances.

item.title: Rent guarantor applications rise 50% since RRA
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act (RRA) has led to a significant shift in the rental market, with a notable 50% increase in guarantor applications, according to recent data from Housing Hand. This surge highlights the growing challenges faced by tenants in securing rental properties, particularly in a market where affordability and tenant protections are under increasing scrutiny.

Understanding the Rise in Guarantor Applications

Guarantor applications have seen a sharp uptick since the Renters’ Rights Act came into effect. The legislation, designed to bolster tenant protections, has inadvertently placed additional pressure on renters. Landlords, now facing stricter regulations, are increasingly seeking financial assurances from tenants. For many, this means requiring a guarantor—a third party who agrees to cover rental payments if the tenant defaults.

This trend reflects the broader challenges in the rental market, where rising rents and tighter affordability checks are making it harder for tenants to meet landlord requirements. Young professionals, students, and those with limited credit history are particularly affected, often needing a guarantor to secure a tenancy.

The Impact of the Renters’ Rights Act

The Renters’ Rights Act was introduced to improve conditions for tenants, offering greater security and fairness in the rental market. However, its implementation has had unintended consequences. Whilst the act has provided tenants with more rights, it has also led to landlords adopting stricter criteria to mitigate potential risks.

As a result, guarantor applications have become more common, with Housing Hand reporting a substantial rise in demand for their services. This suggests that whilst the act aims to protect tenants, it may also be creating barriers for those who struggle to meet the enhanced financial requirements now being imposed by landlords.

What This Means for Tenants and Landlords

For tenants, the increase in guarantor applications underscores the importance of financial planning and preparation when entering the rental market. Those without a guarantor may find it increasingly difficult to secure a property, particularly in competitive areas.

Landlords, on the other hand, are navigating a more regulated environment. Whilst the Renters’ Rights Act offers greater protections for tenants, landlords are seeking ways to safeguard their investments. Requiring a guarantor is one approach, but it may also narrow the pool of potential tenants, particularly in markets where affordability is already a concern.

The rise in guarantor applications highlights the complexities of the UK rental market. Whilst the Renters’ Rights Act aims to improve tenant protections, its implementation has led to new challenges for both renters and landlords. As the market continues to evolve, both parties may need to adapt to these changing dynamics to ensure a fair and sustainable rental landscape.

Auction House has been crowned Auction House of the Year, marking a significant achievement in the property auction sector. item.title: Property group targets £10m agency acquisition spree with eight deals in pipeline
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The property group Sourced has announced plans to invest a minimum of £10 million in acquiring estate and letting agencies across the UK. With eight deals already in progress and four completed this year, the company is ramping up its acquisition strategy, aiming to finalise most transactions by the end of 2026. This move highlights the growing trend of consolidation within the property sector, as independent agency owners increasingly consider succession planning and the challenges of adapting to technological advancements.

Focus on Established Agencies

Sourced is targeting well-established estate and letting agencies with recurring revenue streams and experienced teams. The company emphasises that the £10 million investment represents a starting point rather than a cap, with scope for further acquisitions if suitable opportunities arise. Each potential deal will undergo thorough financial, legal, and operational due diligence to ensure alignment with Sourced’s broader strategy.

One notable acquisition this year was Open House, which brought 104 franchisees into the Sourced network. This deal underscores the company’s commitment to expanding its footprint and strengthening its position in the market. By integrating established agencies, Sourced aims to create a robust portfolio that can navigate the evolving landscape of the property sector.

AI Concerns Influence Succession Planning

According to Sourced CEO Stephen Moss, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming a factor in the decision-making process for independent agency owners. While some see AI as an opportunity to innovate, others are concerned about the financial and operational investment required to stay competitive. Moss noted that many owners have already invested significant time and resources adapting to regulatory changes and technological advancements. The prospect of another major shift, driven by AI, is prompting some to reconsider their long-term plans.

“AI is now a recurring theme in our discussions with agency owners,” Moss explained. “While some are excited about the potential benefits, others worry about falling behind if they don’t continually invest in new systems. For many, the question is whether they want to dedicate the next five to ten years to keeping pace with these changes.”

It’s worth noting that the agencies entering the market are not necessarily struggling financially. Moss highlighted that many are performing well, but their owners feel ready for a new chapter in their lives. This sentiment is driving a wave of acquisitions, as Sourced positions itself as a partner for owners considering retirement or succession.

Ongoing Acquisition Strategy

Sourced’s acquisition programme is expected to extend beyond its current pipeline, with the £10 million investment serving as a foundation rather than a limit. The company is actively seeking opportunities to engage with agency owners who are contemplating selling their businesses or planning for retirement in the coming years. Moss reiterated that Sourced has the appetite and resources to invest further if the right opportunities arise.

The property sector is undergoing a period of significant consolidation, with independent agencies weighing up the costs of regulation, technology, and succession planning. Sourced’s strategy reflects this broader trend, as it seeks to build a resilient and forward-thinking network of agencies capable of thriving in an increasingly competitive market.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, these developments could lead to a more streamlined and technologically advanced property market. As Sourced continues its acquisition spree, the focus on innovation and consolidation may shape the future of estate and letting agencies across the UK.

item.title: Buyer numbers rise but lengthy sales and rental shortages squeeze market
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property market showed tentative signs of recovery in July, with rising buyer interest but persistent challenges around lengthy sales processes and rental shortages, according to latest industry figures. While estate agents reported increased registrations from prospective purchasers, the market continues to favour buyers with considerable negotiating power.

Buyer demand rises but power balance remains

Propertymark's July data revealed estate agents registered an average of 75 new prospective buyers per branch - suggesting underlying demand remains in the housing market. The professional body also noted modest improvements in both sales agreed and new property instructions.

However, with an average of nearly 11 properties available per branch, stock levels continue to build. This buyer's market environment means most homes are selling below asking price, maintaining strong negotiating positions for purchasers. Industry experts suggest realistic pricing has become crucial as buyers adopt more cautious approaches.

Conveyancing delays persist

The sales process continues to face significant delays, with over half of agents reporting most transactions taking 17 weeks or longer from accepted offer to exchange. These protracted timescales are creating uncertainty in the market and potentially undermining confidence.

Propertymark's CEO Nathan Emerson commented: "While July's figures show encouraging activity, challenges remain. The conveyancing process delays are particularly concerning, creating unnecessary hurdles in an otherwise functional market."

Rental market pressures intensify

The lettings sector paints an even starker picture, with severe supply-demand imbalances continuing. Letting agents agreed an average of just over eight new tenancies per branch in July, while facing nine prospective tenants competing for each available property.

Emerson noted: "The rental market's fundamental imbalance persists, with affordability remaining a critical issue despite some moderation in rental growth. The rise in rental arrears further highlights the financial pressures many households face."

For homeowners considering selling, the current market conditions may require patience and realistic pricing expectations. Meanwhile, prospective buyers might find opportunities to negotiate favourable terms, though they should prepare for potentially lengthy transaction times. In the rental sector, tenants continue to face intensely competitive conditions with limited available properties.

item.title: The biggest barrier to getting the property market moving revealed
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research highlights that the cost of moving, rather than mortgage rates, is the primary obstacle preventing homeowners from entering or accelerating their property transactions. According to a study by LRG, 75% of respondents stated that reducing the overall expense of moving would motivate them to move sooner. Meanwhile, 34% emphasised the importance of greater certainty that an agreed sale would complete, and 30% called for a simpler, less stressful process. Interestingly, only 28% cited lower mortgage rates as a key factor, though this figure masks a notable generational divide.

The generational gap in moving priorities

The survey revealed stark differences between younger and older movers. Among those under 45, 70% said lower mortgage rates would encourage them to move, compared to just 13% of respondents aged 55 and over. Conversely, 39% of over-55s prioritised certainty that a sale would complete, while only 23% of younger respondents felt the same. As older homeowners made up a larger proportion of the survey sample, their priorities significantly influenced the overall findings.

For younger buyers, higher borrowing costs remain a pressing concern. Zoopla’s August House Price Index reported that the average five-year fixed mortgage rate stood at around 4.8% in late August, up from below 4% at the start of the year. This increase has reduced borrowing power significantly, with someone able to borrow £200,000 in January now limited to approximately £182,000 for the same monthly repayment. Despite these affordability pressures, buyer interest has remained resilient, with home searches 7% higher than the same period last year.

Certainty and fall-through concerns

Transaction uncertainty has also emerged as a major worry for movers, particularly older homeowners. Around 18% of respondents cited chains, delays, or sales falling through as nearly preventing them from moving. Neil Louth, group executive director of LRG and CEO of The Acorn Group, explained: “Many older movers have both the equity and a genuine reason to move, but they place much greater importance on certainty once a sale has been agreed. People do not want to commit time and money only to see the transaction fall apart.”

Louth added that affordability remains a key concern, especially for younger buyers, but emphasised that mortgage rates are only one part of the decision-making process. Homeowners are increasingly considering the overall cost and value of moving, which includes factors such as transaction certainty and the efficiency of the process.

As the property market navigates these challenges, addressing the cost of moving and improving transaction reliability could play a crucial role in encouraging more homeowners to take the leap. With generational priorities shaping the market, tailored solutions may be needed to meet the diverse needs of buyers and sellers alike.

item.title: CGT fears grow as investors brace for potential Budget tax rise
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Property investors are keeping a close eye on the upcoming Budget as speculation mounts over potential changes to capital gains tax (CGT). With the government reportedly exploring ways to boost revenue, rumours of aligning CGT rates more closely with income tax have sparked concern among landlords and investors. While no official announcements have been made, the uncertainty could influence decisions around property sales.

Budget Speculation Fuels CGT Concerns

The government is under pressure to address public finances, with public sector borrowing reaching £18.3bn in August, significantly higher than forecasts. This has led to discussions about potential tax reforms, including adjustments to CGT. Reports suggest that ministers may consider raising the personal income tax allowance, which could necessitate finding additional revenue streams elsewhere. CGT, often seen as a lucrative source, has become a focal point of these discussions.

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, noted that tax speculation is intensifying ahead of the Budget. She highlighted that if the government reduces income tax burdens, it may need to compensate by increasing taxes like CGT. This has left property investors in a state of uncertainty, with many weighing the implications of potential tax hikes on their portfolios.

Potential Impact on Property Investors

For landlords and property investors, a rise in CGT could lead to significant changes in behaviour. Higher tax rates might prompt some to delay selling assets to avoid increased liabilities. This could result in a slowdown in property disposals, particularly among those assessing the financial impact of the changes. Streeter emphasised that while tax considerations are important, they should not dictate broader investment strategies. She advised against letting “the tax tail wag the investment dog,” urging investors to remain focused on long-term goals rather than speculative tax changes.

However, the prospect of a higher CGT bill remains a pressing concern for many. Investors may wish to review their portfolios and seek professional advice to understand how potential changes could affect their financial plans. With the Budget announcement looming, staying informed and prepared could help mitigate any adverse impacts.

Looking Ahead

As the government finalises its Budget plans, property investors are advised to monitor developments closely. While speculation about CGT changes persists, nothing has been confirmed, and any adjustments would require careful consideration. In the meantime, investors might consider exploring their options and preparing for various scenarios to ensure they remain well-positioned, regardless of the outcome.

The coming weeks will be crucial for understanding the government’s approach to taxation and its implications for the property market. With careful planning and a proactive mindset, investors can navigate the uncertainty and make informed decisions tailored to their financial objectives.

item.title: Is your estate agency invisible to AI? New research reveals the risk
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research suggests that estate agents could face challenges in maintaining visibility as artificial intelligence (AI) platforms increasingly influence property searches. A study analysing over 10,000 responses from popular AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI Overviews found that these platforms typically recommend just three to five agencies, creating a competitive landscape for agents. The findings highlight how AI-led searches may reshape how buyers and sellers shortlist estate agents, potentially excluding firms that fail to secure a spot in these automated recommendations.

How AI Platforms Influence Property Searches

The research, conducted by Schutle, examined 116 property-related prompts across London, Dubai, and Marbella. It revealed that AI platforms generate tailored recommendations based on factors such as location, customer nationality, and specific requirements. For instance, Knight Frank appeared in 63.8% of responses for Central London, while Hurford Salvi Carr dominated searches in Canary Wharf and Docklands. In Marbella, Engel & Völkers featured prominently for German buyers, whereas Bromley Estates Marbella was the top choice for British buyers. These variations suggest that AI tools are not simply replicating generic search results but are influenced by nuanced customer profiles.

Visibility Challenges for Estate Agents

One of the most significant findings is that visibility on one AI platform does not guarantee prominence on others. For example, Dubai-based Harbor Real Estate appeared in 95 responses on ChatGPT but only 15 on Gemini and none on Google AI Overviews. This inconsistency means estate agents cannot rely on a single AI service to boost their visibility. Independent agents, in particular, may face an uphill battle to compete with larger, internationally recognised brands, though the study showed that smaller firms can outperform bigger names in specific markets.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property and mortgage sectors have seen notable movements in recent weeks, with professionals taking on new roles and stepping into fresh challenges. These changes highlight the dynamic nature of the industry and its ability to attract and retain top talent.

Savills Welcomes Back Experienced Consultant

Savills has announced the return of Iain Powis, who rejoins the firm as an associate director in its residential development sales team in Oxford. Powis brings almost two decades of property industry experience, including an 11-year stint at Savills earlier in his career. After three years in senior roles at independent property businesses, Powis is back to advise housebuilders, developers, landowners, and institutional clients across Oxfordshire and surrounding areas.

Reflecting on his return, Powis commented, “After more than a decade with Savills earlier in my career, I am excited to rejoin the residential development sales team in Oxford. The collaborative culture and the team’s strong reputation were key factors in my decision to return.” Nicola Horner, regional head of Savills Residential Development Sales, praised Powis’s expertise, stating, “Iain’s deep understanding of the Oxfordshire market and his strategic approach to residential development make him a valuable addition to our team.”

Zoopla COO Steps Down

Meanwhile, Zoopla’s chief operating officer, Rich Hayes, has decided to leave the property portal after three years. Hayes, who also co-founded Mojo Mortgages, plans to focus on his own business interests, including roles as a strategic adviser and non-executive director. A Zoopla spokesperson acknowledged his contributions, saying, “Rich leaves to pursue his ambition of leading a business again. We thank him for his dedication and wish him well.”

Hayes joined Zoopla’s senior leadership team prior to Paul Whitehead’s appointment as CEO in March 2025. During his tenure, Hayes oversaw the portal’s day-to-day operations, playing a pivotal role in its growth and development. Zoopla has yet to announce a replacement for the COO position.

These appointments and departures underscore the evolving landscape of the UK property and mortgage sectors. For homeowners and industry professionals alike, such movements often signal new opportunities and fresh perspectives in an ever-changing market.

item.title: Property investors face 45% capital gains tax as Labour weighs major hike
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Property investors in the UK could face significant changes to their tax obligations as proposals to align capital gains tax (CGT) with income tax rates gain traction. Reports suggest that CGT rates might rise to as much as 45%, a move that could reshape investor behaviour and impact the property market. Whilst the government has yet to confirm any changes, the potential implications are already sparking debate among experts.

What Are the Proposed Changes?

Currently, individuals pay CGT at rates of 18% or 24%, depending on their taxable income and gains. However, proposals put forward by Labour donor and Ecotricity founder Dale Vince suggest aligning CGT more closely with income tax rates, potentially increasing it to 45%. The additional revenue generated from this change could be used to raise the income tax personal allowance from £12,570 to £15,570, a move aimed at supporting lower earners.

Estimates suggest that aligning CGT with income tax could generate around £14bn in revenue. However, concerns have been raised about whether this approach would deliver the expected financial boost. Jessica Partridge, partner and head of tax and trusts at Mayo Wynne Baxter, highlights that higher tax rates do not always result in proportionately higher revenues, as taxpayers may alter their behaviour to reduce exposure.

How Could This Affect Property Investors?

A sharp increase in CGT could have significant implications for landlords and other property investors. Higher rates might influence decisions around when to sell assets, potentially leading to delays in property disposals or a tendency to retain investments for longer periods. This could, in turn, affect the number and timing of investment property sales in the market.

Jessica Partridge warns that capital is highly mobile, and taxpayers often adjust their strategies in response to tax changes. Investors might explore restructuring their affairs or delaying sales to mitigate their tax liabilities. Such shifts in behaviour could reduce the anticipated revenue from higher CGT rates, making it a less reliable source of income for the government.

Broader Implications for the UK Tax System

Aligning CGT with income tax would represent a fundamental shift in the UK’s approach to taxing investment and wealth creation. Proponents argue that it could create a fairer system by reducing disparities between different forms of income. However, critics highlight the potential unintended consequences, such as reduced investment activity and changes in taxpayer behaviour.

Whilst the proposal may appear attractive, especially if the proceeds are used to support lower earners, its success hinges on whether the projected revenues materialise. History suggests that higher CGT rates do not always translate into proportionately higher tax receipts, raising questions about the long-term viability of such a policy.

As the government considers these proposals ahead of the upcoming Budget, property investors and stakeholders in the housing market will be closely monitoring developments. Any changes to CGT rates could have far-reaching effects, influencing investment decisions and shaping the future of the UK property landscape.

item.title: Portfolio landlords turn to agents as self-management gets tougher
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

With the regulatory landscape for landlords becoming increasingly complex, many portfolio landlords are reconsidering the practicality of self-managing their rental properties. Recent research highlights that nearly three-quarters (74%) of self-managing landlords have found property management more challenging over the past three years, with 57% citing recent legislative changes as a key factor in their decision-making process. This shift could lead to growing demand for professional letting and management services.

The Growing Burden of Compliance

Compliance has emerged as the primary source of stress for landlords, with 41% identifying it as their biggest pressure point. This surpasses concerns around maintenance and repairs (20%), changes between tenancies (11%), and tenant communication (10%). The introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act and other regulatory requirements has intensified the focus on adherence to legislation, prompting landlords to reassess their management strategies.

For many, the complexity of staying abreast of legal changes has become overwhelming. Roma Sharma, managing director of Rushbrook, notes, “The legislative landscape has become considerably more demanding, and the Renters’ Rights Act has only increased the focus on getting things right.” This has led some landlords to question whether self-management remains the most viable option.

Time Pressures and Practical Challenges

Maintenance and repairs, rather than compliance, consume the majority of landlords’ time. Over half (52%) of respondents identified these tasks as the most time-intensive aspect of property management. Additionally, 68% of landlords spend at least 31 hours per month managing their portfolios, with a further 17% dedicating between 21 and 30 hours.

This workload often results in delays to non-urgent repairs, with 77% of landlords admitting they postpone such tasks due to time constraints. For those with larger portfolios—62% own six or more properties, and 36% own at least 11—the demands of self-management can be particularly taxing.

The Role of Letting and Managing Agents

As landlords grapple with these challenges, many are turning to professional agents for support. When asked why they might consider outsourcing management, 26% cited the need to stay compliant with legislation, while 21% highlighted the desire to save time. Reducing stress (15%) and managing tenant relationships (11%) were also key factors, alongside handling maintenance and repairs (9%).

Letting and managing agents are well-positioned to alleviate these pressures, offering expertise in compliance, maintenance coordination, and tenant communication. For landlords facing mounting responsibilities, outsourcing management could provide a practical solution to navigate the evolving rental landscape.

As the regulatory environment continues to evolve, landlords may find it increasingly beneficial to seek professional support. With compliance and time management posing significant challenges, partnering with letting and managing agents could help landlords streamline their operations and focus on growing their portfolios.

item.title: EYE POLL: Will the new national landlord register improve the private rented sector?
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK government is introducing a national landlord register, aiming to enhance transparency and address issues of non-compliance in the private rented sector. This new initiative is set to impact both landlords and letting agents, but opinions are divided on whether it will truly improve standards or simply add another layer of bureaucracy.

What is the national landlord register?

The national landlord register is a government-backed scheme designed to create a comprehensive database of landlords operating in the private rented sector. By requiring landlords to register and pay an annual fee of £65, the initiative seeks to improve accountability and ensure compliance with existing regulations. Proponents argue that it will help identify rogue operators and raise overall standards, whilst critics suggest it could place an unnecessary burden on responsible landlords and agents.

Potential benefits of the register

Supporters of the scheme believe it could bring significant improvements to the private rented sector. By creating a centralised database, local authorities and letting agents may find it easier to identify landlords who fail to meet their legal obligations. This could lead to more effective enforcement of existing regulations, potentially reducing issues such as poor property maintenance and unfair evictions. Additionally, tenants might benefit from greater transparency, as they could verify whether their landlord is registered and compliant with the law.

Concerns and criticisms

However, not everyone is convinced of the register’s merits. Some argue that the £65 annual fee is excessive, particularly for smaller landlords who already face rising costs. Others question whether the scheme will add meaningful value, suggesting that existing regulations should be enforced more rigorously instead. Critics also warn that the register could create unnecessary bureaucracy, placing additional strain on landlords and agents who already adhere to the rules. The effectiveness of the scheme will likely depend on how it is implemented and managed.

As the national landlord register moves forward, homeowners and industry professionals may wish to stay informed about its progress and implications. Whilst the initiative aims to improve standards in the private rented sector, its success will hinge on balancing transparency with practicality.

item.title: Council scraps £1,500 HMO licensing plans after legal challenge
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Telford and Wrekin Council has abandoned plans to extend its Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMO) licensing scheme, sparing landlords additional fees of up to £1,500 per property. The proposed changes would have required smaller shared properties with three or four occupants to meet additional licensing requirements. However, following consultation and a legal challenge from the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA), the council has revoked the designation, effective from 15 September 2026.

Why Were the Plans Scrapped?

The NRLA raised significant concerns about the council’s consultation process, arguing that key documents were not properly publicised or provided during the review. The association also questioned the legal basis for certain charges and claimed the council had failed to adequately address landlord concerns. Initially, the council disputed the NRLA’s position but later proposed addressing some of the issues raised. Ultimately, however, it decided to withdraw the scheme entirely.

Ben Beadle, chief executive of the NRLA, welcomed the decision, stating that the association had been prepared to challenge the designation in court if concerns remained unresolved. He emphasised the importance of avoiding unnecessary duplication of costs and administrative burdens, particularly with the impending introduction of a national landlord database.

What’s Next for Landlords?

The withdrawal of Telford and Wrekin’s additional licensing scheme coincides with the launch of the government’s national landlord database, set to take effect in the West Midlands from 15 December 2026. The abandoned local scheme would have overlapped with these new national requirements, potentially requiring landlords to submit similar compliance information twice.

The NRLA has urged councils to carefully consider the impact of introducing local schemes that duplicate national efforts without offering clear benefits. Landlords may wish to stay informed about upcoming changes, particularly the introduction of the national database, to ensure they remain compliant with evolving regulations.

What Does This Mean for the Rental Market?

The decision to scrap the additional HMO licensing scheme could provide some relief for landlords facing rising costs and regulatory pressures. However, the introduction of the national landlord database highlights the government’s ongoing focus on improving standards and transparency in the private rental sector.

Landlords operating in Telford and Wrekin, as well as across the West Midlands, might consider reviewing their compliance processes ahead of the database’s launch. Staying proactive could help avoid potential penalties and ensure a smoother transition to the new system.

As the rental market continues to evolve, both landlords and tenants may benefit from clearer, more streamlined regulations. However, striking the right balance between oversight and affordability remains a key challenge for policymakers.
